screens.title: Introduction to Unity UI (uGUI)
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you will learn the foundational pieces that make Unity's built-in UI system work. We start with the Canvas, the drawing surface that hosts all UI elements, and then move into the Rect Transform which replaces the regular Transform for every UI object. You will learn practical settings such as the Canvas render modes and how they determine whether UI sits over the scene or exists within world space. Anchors and pivots are core ideas you will master; anchors let elements stick to positions relative to a parent, while pivots determine the rotation and scaling origin for an element. We will also cover common components you create immediately: TextMeshPro for crisp text, Image for sprites and backgrounds, and Button for interactive controls. Finally, you will learn about the Canvas Scaler and why choosing Scale With Screen Size early saves a lot of rework when you test different resolutions. A concrete outcome: by the end you'll be able to build a basic, responsive main menu using the techniques shown here. Notice one common trap: forgetting to configure anchors and Canvas Scaler leads to UIs that look right in one window and break in another. Keep that in mind as you follow the step-by-step examples that come next.

screens.title: Canvas — the UI drawing surface
screens.narratorSegment: The Canvas is the fundamental GameObject that renders all UI in Unity. Think of it as the paper on which UI elements are painted. There are three render modes you should know. Screen Space - Overlay places UI above everything in the scene and is the simplest for menus and HUDs. Screen Space - Camera renders the Canvas through a chosen camera, which lets you apply camera effects or match perspective. World Space makes UI behave like any other 3D object in the scene, useful for floating health bars or in-world panels that interact with the environment. A concrete example: use Overlay for a main menu that must stay fixed to the screen, use Camera mode if you want UI to receive post-processing from a camera, and use World Space for a nameplate above an NPC. A common mistake is creating UI elements without noticing the Canvas render mode; placing a button expecting to be part of the world but leaving Canvas as Overlay will make it always face the screen instead of sitting in 3D space. Key practical steps: when you add a UI element and Unity creates a Canvas automatically, immediately check the Canvas component and Canvas Scaler so elements behave as you expect. To check understanding, try switching a Canvas between Overlay and World Space with the same child elements and watch how their behavior changes.

keyIdea.title: Canvas in one line
keyIdea.text: Canvas defines how UI is rendered: overlay for screen-fixed, camera for camera-tied, world space for 3D-integrated UI.

content.html:
Core Concept › Canvas
Canvas and render modes
The Canvas controls how child UI is drawn and interacts with cameras or the world.
Screen Space - Overlay
Renders UI on top of the scene. Use for menus and HUDs; scales with Canvas Scaler.
Screen Space - Camera
Renders through a camera. Useful for applying camera effects to UI or matching perspective.
World Space
Makes UI a 3D object in the scene. Good for in-world panels and indicators.
Example
A pause menu uses Screen Space - Overlay so it always appears above game content regardless of camera position.
Common mistake
Adding world UI but leaving Canvas in Overlay means your UI will not behave like a 3D object. Always verify Canvas mode after creating UI elements.
Key Takeaway

Choose Canvas render mode based on whether UI should be screen-fixed or part of the game world.

screens.title: Rect Transform — UI geometry and layout
screens.narratorSegment: Rect Transform is the specialized transform used by all UI elements in Unity. Unlike the regular Transform with position, rotation, and scale in 3D space, Rect Transform defines a rectangle with explicit width and height, and includes anchors, offsets, and pivot properties. These additional fields let you express layout intentions relative to a parent Rect Transform. For example, Left, Right, Top and Bottom offsets let you set margins when anchors are set to stretch. Anchors are defined by Anchor Min and Anchor Max values which reference positions on the parent rectangle. Pivots are normalized points inside the element that determine where rotation and scaling originate. A concrete example: a health bar can have anchors fixed to the top-left corner of a parent panel so its position remains consistent as the screen changes. A common misconception is to treat Rect Transform like a position-only tool; instead, treat it as a layout object—its anchors should be your primary tool when making responsive UIs. To practice, create a UI element, change anchor presets to top-left, stretch horizontally, and observe how the width and offsets react when resizing the Game view. This builds intuition for how anchors and offsets combine to control final position and size.

keyIdea.title: Rect Transform role
keyIdea.text: Rect Transform combines size, anchors, offsets, and pivot to express 2D UI layout relative to a parent.

content.html:
Definition › Rect Transform
Rect Transform properties
Keys: Width, Height, Anchor Min/Max, Left/Right/Top/Bottom offsets, and Pivot.
Anchors
Define reference points on the parent. Use corners or stretch presets to control how a child resizes.
Offsets
Left/Right/Top/Bottom are margins that take effect once anchors are set.
Pivot
Normalized point inside the rectangle used as the rotation and scale origin.
Quick exercise
Create an Image, set anchors to Top-Left, then resize the Game view. Observe how Pos X, Pos Y, and offsets change while the element stays in the corner.
Misconception
Treating Rect Transform like a regular Transform. Remember it encodes layout relationships not only a position vector.
Key Takeaway

Use anchors to declare layout behavior and offsets for margins; pivot affects rotation and scaling origin.

screens.title: Anchors and Pivots — practical rules
screens.narratorSegment: Anchors and pivots together determine how a UI element moves and scales when its parent changes size. Start by asking: should this element stick to a corner, stretch along an edge, or remain centered? If you want a bottom-right element, set Anchor Min and Anchor Max both to (1, 0). That pins the element’s reference to the bottom-right corner of the parent. For a header that should stretch horizontally, set Anchor Min X to 0 and Anchor Max X to 1 while keeping Y anchored to the top; this makes width follow the parent while preserving top offset margins. Pivots are independent and usually set to 0.5,0.5 for centered scaling, or 0,1 for top-left rotation origin. A concrete workflow: 1) Choose anchor preset that expresses the desired relationship. 2) Adjust Pos X/Pos Y or Left/Right/Top/Bottom offsets to position with margins. 3) Set pivot to control rotation and scale origin. A common mistake is moving an element visually and forgetting to update anchors, which leaves the element with center anchors and leads to unexpected jumps when the parent scales. Test by resizing the Game view and observing whether the element keeps its intended relation. This practice creates robust, responsive layouts without needing manual repositioning for each resolution.

content.html:
Process Flow › Anchors & Pivots
Workflow
  1. Choose anchor preset. Corner, edge, or stretch expresses layout intent.
  2. Set offsets. Use Pos or Left/Right/Top/Bottom to apply margins relative to anchors.
  3. Adjust pivot. Decide how the element will rotate or scale by picking its pivot point.
  4. Test. Resize the Game view to confirm behavior across resolutions.
Concrete example
To pin a menu button to bottom-right, set both Anchor Min and Anchor Max to (1,0), then set Pos X to -50 and Pos Y to 50 so it offsets inward from the corner.
Common mistake
Moving elements while anchors remain centered. This causes elements to shift unexpectedly when the parent changes size.
Key Takeaway

Set anchors first to express relationship, then use offsets; pivot controls rotation and scale origin.

screens.title: Create Text and TextMeshPro
screens.narratorSegment: TextMeshPro delivers crisp rendered text and is the recommended component for all UI text. When you add a TextMeshPro element for the first time, Unity prompts you to import the TextMeshPro essentials — do that immediately. After import, create a Text - TextMeshPro element from the UI menu. Set its anchors depending on how you want the text to behave: Top-Center for titles, Center for centered labels, or stretch presets for multi-line bodies. Configure width and height in the Rect Transform; avoid embedding excessive content into a single line. Use the Inspector to set font size, color, and alignment. A concrete example: add a TitleText element, anchor it Top-Center, set Pos Y to -100, and make width about 800 with height 150. This gives consistent placement across resolutions when paired with a Canvas Scaler. A common misconception is that increasing font size alone solves readability on high-resolution displays. In practice, TextMeshPro uses signed distance fields so text remains sharp at different scales; pair it with Canvas Scaler set to Scale With Screen Size to preserve intended visual proportions. After creating text, verify in Game view at multiple resolutions to ensure line wrapping and alignment behave as expected.

keyIdea.title: Text practice
keyIdea.text: Use TextMeshPro for high-quality text. Anchor titles and test across resolutions for readable results.

content.html:
Process › Text & TextMeshPro
Steps to add high-quality UI text
  1. Right-click Hierarchy → UI → Text - TextMeshPro and import essentials when prompted.
  2. Set Anchor preset to Top-Center for titles and adjust Pos Y to position vertically.
  3. Set Width and Height in Rect Transform to control wrapping and alignment.
  4. Adjust font size, color, and alignment in the Inspector; prefer TextMeshPro for clarity across scales.
Concrete example
Create TitleText, anchors Top-Center, Pos Y -100, Width 800, Height 150. Set text to "My Awesome Game" and check in 1920x1080 and 1280x720 Game views.
Misconception
Relying on legacy UI Text causes blurry scaling. Use TextMeshPro and Canvas Scaler instead.
Key Takeaway

Import TextMeshPro essentials, anchor titles appropriately, and confirm readability across resolutions.

screens.title: Image and Button setup
screens.narratorSegment: Images and Buttons are the visual building blocks of menus and HUDs. To add a background image, right-click Canvas → UI → Image and drag a Sprite into the Source Image field in the Inspector. For backgrounds that must cover the entire screen, set anchors to stretch (Anchor Min 0,0 and Anchor Max 1,1) and set Left/Right/Top/Bottom to zero. Buttons are created via UI → Button - TextMeshPro and combine an Image for the background with a child TextMeshPro label. You can customize the button's Image sprite for different visual styles, and adjust transition settings if you want hover or press feedback. A practical example: create a Play button, set its anchors to Center-Center, set Width 200 and Height 60, and change the child TextMeshPro to say "Play Game." A common mistake is placing the TextMeshPro label outside the button hierarchy or forgetting to assign a sprite to the Image, which results in an invisible button. Always verify that the label is a child of the button and that the button's Image has a valid sprite or color. Finally, test the button in Play mode to ensure visual states and click targets behave as expected.

keyIdea.title: Button essentials
keyIdea.text: Buttons combine an Image background and a TextMeshPro child label; anchors and hierarchy determine visibility and placement.

content.html:
Process › Image & Button
Adding an Image
Right-click Canvas → UI → Image. Drag a sprite into Source Image. Use stretch anchors for full-screen backgrounds with zero offsets.
Creating a Button
Right-click Canvas → UI → Button - TextMeshPro. Ensure the TextMeshPro label is a child of the button and assign a sprite or color to the Image component.
Concrete example
PlayButton: Anchor Center-Center, Pos Y -100, Width 200, Height 60, child text "Play Game". Assign a rounded sprite to the Image for better visuals.
Common mistake
Putting the label outside the button's hierarchy or forgetting the button Image sprite makes the button invisible or non-interactive.
Key Takeaway

Buttons require both an Image background and a properly nested label; anchors determine placement and stretching.

screens.title: UI Hierarchy and draw order
screens.narratorSegment: The UI Hierarchy in Unity determines draw order and grouping. By default, siblings later in the Hierarchy draw on top of earlier siblings. That means to ensure text appears above a background image, place the Text element after or as a child of a container that sits above the Image. Group related elements under an empty GameObject parent such as MainMenuPanel or PlayerHUD to apply shared transforms, anchor sets, and Canvas override behaviors. Parents define coordinate systems for their children through their Rect Transforms; moving or scaling a parent affects all children, which is a powerful way to manage whole panels. A common pitfall is placing a panel under the wrong parent and then wondering why it moves when another object moves. A practical example: create a PlayerHUD parent anchored to the top of the screen, then add health and score as children. Anchoring the parent to top-left keeps all children consistent. Also remember EventSystem appears when you add interactive UI and should remain present for button clicks to work. To check your understanding, rearrange a small set of UI elements and predict which will render on top; then run the scene and verify that draw order matches the Hierarchy.

content.html:
Hierarchy › Draw Order & Groups
Draw order behavior
Siblings later in the Hierarchy render on top of earlier siblings. Use this to ensure labels appear above images.
Grouping strategy
Group related elements under an empty parent to share anchors and transforms. Example: MainMenuPanel or PlayerHUD.
Concrete example
Place Background Image, then TitleText, then PlayButton in that order. The PlayButton will render on top if it appears later in the Hierarchy.
Tip
Use parent panels to move or animate multiple UI elements together rather than adjusting each child individually.
Key Takeaway

Hierarchy order controls rendering; group UI logically to simplify layout adjustments and scaling.

screens.title: Canvas Scaler modes
screens.narratorSegment: The Canvas Scaler controls how UI elements scale as the screen size changes. Constant Pixel Size makes elements keep the same pixel dimensions regardless of resolution. This can be useful for pixel-perfect UIs but often leads to elements appearing too small on high-density displays or too large on low resolutions. Scale With Screen Size is generally recommended for responsive game UIs. It uses a Reference Resolution and scales UI based on the current screen resolution relative to that reference. Screen Match Mode, such as Match Width Or Height, controls whether scaling favors width, height, or a mix using the Match slider. For example, with a reference of 1920 x 1080 and Match set to 0.5, Unity balances scaling between width and height so UIs maintain proportions across common aspect ratios. A common pitfall is leaving Canvas Scaler on Constant Pixel Size for a cross-platform project, which produces inconsistent UI sizing across devices. To practice, set the Canvas Scaler to Scale With Screen Size, try Reference 1920x1080, and switch between 16:9 and 4:3 Game view resolutions to see how elements scale and where you might need to adjust anchors or match settings.

content.html:
Comparison › Canvas Scaler Modes
Constant Pixel Size
Elements keep exact pixel dimensions. Good for fixed-resolution or pixel-art projects but risky for multi-resolution targets.
Scale With Screen Size
Scales UI based on Reference Resolution. Use Match Width Or Height to prioritize an axis and keep proportions consistent.
Concrete test
Set Reference Resolution to 1920x1080 and Match slider to 0.5. Resize the Game view to 1280x720 and 1024x768 to compare scaling behavior.
Common mistake
Not configuring Canvas Scaler early forces later rework of positions, sizes, and text readability when supporting multiple resolutions.

Set Scale With Screen Size and a practical reference resolution early to avoid layout surprises across devices.

screens.title: Responsive layout strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Creating responsive layouts is an iterative process that combines anchors, parent panels, and Canvas Scaler settings. Start by grouping related UI into panels that represent logical units like MainMenuPanel or PlayerHUD. Anchor each panel to the intended screen area: top, bottom, left, or center. Inside a panel, use child anchors to position elements relative to the panel, which simplifies global shifts. Always set Canvas Scaler to Scale With Screen Size and choose a Reference Resolution that matches your target. Then perform multi-resolution tests: switch the Game view resolution between your reference and other target sizes. Watch for overlapping or clipped elements and adjust anchors or use layout components like Horizontal or Vertical Layout Group later if needed. A concrete example: anchor the PlayerHUD panel to the top of the screen, then add a health bar and score as children with relative anchors — resizing will keep them consistent. A common misconception is assuming one-time placement is enough; responsive design requires testing and small iterative adjustments. End each iteration by testing at least three resolutions and, if possible, at different aspect ratios to ensure consistent alignment and legibility.

keyIdea.text: Group UI into anchored panels, set Canvas Scaler early, and test across multiple resolutions to iterate toward a robust layout.

Process › Responsive Layouts
Iteration workflow
  1. Group related UI into parent panels and set anchors for the panel.
  2. Set Canvas Scaler to Scale With Screen Size with a Reference Resolution.
  3. Test in the Game view at multiple resolutions and aspect ratios.
  4. Adjust anchors, offsets, and panel organization until behavior is stable.
Concrete example
PlayerHUD anchored to top, health bar anchored left in the panel, score anchored right. Changing resolution keeps elements in place because the panel keeps its anchor relationship.
Testing tip
Use at least three resolutions: reference, a narrower width, and a taller height. This quickly reveals anchor and scaling problems.
Key Takeaway

Design by panels and test iteratively; anchors plus Canvas Scaler are your main tools for responsive UI.

screens.title: Common pitfalls and fixes
screens.narratorSegment: Beginners often run into a predictable set of issues when starting with Unity UI. One is forgetting to import TextMeshPro essentials, resulting in missing fonts or warnings. Fix: import the essentials immediately after adding a TextMeshPro element. Another is leaving the Canvas Scaler on Constant Pixel Size for cross-platform projects; the fix is to switch to Scale With Screen Size and pick an appropriate reference resolution. A third common problem is incorrect anchors: placing elements visually but leaving anchors at center leads to elements drifting when the parent resizes. Fix: set anchors to corners or stretch presets that match the intended behavior. Also, ensure button labels are children of their Button so clicks and visual states work. A practical diagnostic workflow: 1) Confirm a Canvas exists. 2) Check Canvas Scaler mode and reference. 3) Inspect anchors on any element that moves unexpectedly. 4) Validate hierarchy order for draw issues. Each of these checks quickly identifies the cause of the most common UI failures. After applying the fix, always re-test in multiple Game view resolutions to verify the issue is resolved.

Common Pitfalls › Fixes
Missing TextMeshPro assets
Import essentials when prompted to avoid missing fonts and warnings.
Wrong Canvas Scaler
Switch to Scale With Screen Size and set a Reference Resolution to maintain proportional UI across devices.
Incorrect anchors
Set anchors to corners or stretch presets rather than leaving center anchors after repositioning elements.

screens.title: Build a basic main menu
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through building a basic main menu you can test across resolutions. Step 1: create a new Canvas in the Hierarchy. Step 2: select the Canvas and set the Canvas Scaler UI Scale Mode to Scale With Screen Size, Reference Resolution to 1920 by 1080, and Screen Match Mode to Match Width Or Height with the Match slider at 0.5. Step 3: as a child of the Canvas add an Image and set its anchors to stretch with all offsets zero so it becomes a full-screen background. Step 4: add a Text - TextMeshPro element, name it TitleText, set anchors to Top-Center, Pos Y to -100, Width 800 and Height 150, then set the text to your game title. Step 5: add a Button - TextMeshPro, name it PlayButton, set anchors to Center-Center, Pos Y -100, Width 200, Height 60, and change the child TextMeshPro to "Play Game." A common oversight is forgetting to import TextMeshPro essentials or leaving the button label outside the button; confirm the label is nested correctly. Finally, enter Play mode and test several Game view resolutions to ensure your layout keeps the title and button legible and positioned correctly. Reflect: which anchor choices most influenced stability across sizes?

Hands-on Activity › Main Menu
Step-by-step
  1. Create Canvas and set Canvas Scaler to Scale With Screen Size, Reference 1920x1080, Match 0.5.
  2. Add Image child, set anchors to stretch and offsets to zero for full-screen background.
  3. Add Text - TextMeshPro named TitleText, anchors Top-Center, Pos Y -100, Width 800, Height 150.
  4. Add Button - TextMeshPro named PlayButton, anchors Center-Center, Pos Y -100, Width 200, Height 60.
  5. Test in Game view at multiple resolutions and confirm placement and scaling.
Example checklist
Canvas exists, Scaler set, Background stretches, Title anchored Top-Center, Play Button anchored Center-Center, TextMeshPro imported.
Troubleshoot
If text or buttons shift, re-check anchors and ensure the PlayButton label is a child of the Button object.

Follow the steps and validate in multiple Game view resolutions to build a robust main menu quickly.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember

A quick verification is to build the main menu activity and test it at multiple resolutions. These three ideas—Canvas mode, Rect Transform with anchors/pivots, and Canvas Scaler—form the backbone of reliable Unity UI. fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you will learn the foundational pieces that make Unity's built-in UI system work. We start with the Canvas, the drawing surface that hosts all UI elements, and then move into the Rect Transform which replaces the regular Transform for every UI object. You will learn practical settings such as the Canvas render modes and how they determine whether UI sits over the scene or exists within world space. Anchors and pivots are core ideas you will master; anchors let elements stick to positions relative to a parent, while pivots determine the rotation and scaling origin for an element. We will also cover common components you create immediately: TextMeshPro for crisp text, Image for sprites and backgrounds, and Button for interactive controls. Finally, you will learn about the Canvas Scaler and why choosing Scale With Screen Size early saves a lot of rework when you test different resolutions. A concrete outcome: by the end you'll be able to build a basic, responsive main menu using the techniques shown here. Notice one common trap: forgetting to configure anchors and Canvas Scaler leads to UIs that look right in one window and break in another. Keep that in mind as you follow the step-by-step examples that come next.

By the end of this chapter you will have four concrete skills you can verify. First, you will identify and configure the Canvas and its render modes so UI is drawn in the correct context. You will be able to explain when to use Screen Space - Overlay versus Screen Space - Camera or World Space with practical reasons for each. Second, you will create and configure basic UI elements such as TextMeshPro, Image, and Button. That includes importing TextMeshPro essentials and setting sprites for Image components. Third, you will master Anchors and Pivots: how to set Anchor Min and Max and how pivot values affect rotation and scaling, enabling responsive placement. Fourth, you will implement a simple responsive layout and set the Canvas Scaler correctly, choosing Scale With Screen Size, a reference resolution, and a screen match mode to avoid elements stretching incorrectly. Each objective is paired with a milestone you can test in the Game view. As you practice, check for common mistakes such as forgetting the Canvas Scaler or leaving anchors at center when you intended corner alignment. These skills will make your menus reliable across resolutions and platforms.

This second objectives slide focuses on practicing and preventing errors. You will follow a hands-on activity: create a Canvas, set Canvas Scaler to Scale With Screen Size, and build a main menu with a background image, TextMeshPro title, and a center Play button. During practice check that the Image anchor stretches to full screen, the title uses Top-Center anchors, and the play button uses Center-Center anchors with position offsets. You will also learn to test across resolutions in the Game view; resizing the Game window or switching resolutions exposes layout issues early. A common mistake to watch for is leaving anchors at the default center when you intended a corner, which causes elements to move unpredictably when the parent scales. Another frequent oversight is using legacy UI Text instead of TextMeshPro, which leads to blurry text at high resolutions. The milestone here is a responsive main menu that holds its layout across at least two different aspect ratios. Reflect after building: can you identify which anchor choices made the title and button stable across sizes?

The Canvas is the fundamental GameObject that renders all UI in Unity. Think of it as the paper on which UI elements are painted. There are three render modes you should know. Screen Space - Overlay places UI above everything in the scene and is the simplest for menus and HUDs. Screen Space - Camera renders the Canvas through a chosen camera, which lets you apply camera effects or match perspective. World Space makes UI behave like any other 3D object in the scene, useful for floating health bars or in-world panels that interact with the environment. A concrete example: use Overlay for a main menu that must stay fixed to the screen, use Camera mode if you want UI to receive post-processing from a camera, and use World Space for a nameplate above an NPC. A common mistake is creating UI elements without noticing the Canvas render mode; placing a button expecting to be part of the world but leaving Canvas as Overlay will make it always face the screen instead of sitting in 3D space. Key practical steps: when you add a UI element and Unity creates a Canvas automatically, immediately check the Canvas component and Canvas Scaler so elements behave as you expect. To check understanding, try switching a Canvas between Overlay and World Space with the same child elements and watch how their behavior changes.

Rect Transform is the specialized transform used by all UI elements in Unity. Unlike the regular Transform with position, rotation, and scale in 3D space, Rect Transform defines a rectangle with explicit width and height, and includes anchors, offsets, and pivot properties. These additional fields let you express layout intentions relative to a parent Rect Transform. For example, Left, Right, Top and Bottom offsets let you set margins when anchors are set to stretch. Anchors are defined by Anchor Min and Anchor Max values which reference positions on the parent rectangle. Pivots are normalized points inside the element that determine where rotation and scaling originate. A concrete example: a health bar can have anchors fixed to the top-left corner of a parent panel so its position remains consistent as the screen changes. A common misconception is to treat Rect Transform like a position-only tool; instead, treat it as a layout object—its anchors should be your primary tool when making responsive UIs. To practice, create a UI element, change anchor presets to top-left, stretch horizontally, and observe how the width and offsets react when resizing the Game view. This builds intuition for how anchors and offsets combine to control final position and size.

Anchors and pivots together determine how a UI element moves and scales when its parent changes size. Start by asking: should this element stick to a corner, stretch along an edge, or remain centered? If you want a bottom-right element, set Anchor Min and Anchor Max both to (1, 0). That pins the element’s reference to the bottom-right corner of the parent. For a header that should stretch horizontally, set Anchor Min X to 0 and Anchor Max X to 1 while keeping Y anchored to the top; this makes width follow the parent while preserving top offset margins. Pivots are independent and usually set to 0.5,0.5 for centered scaling, or 0,1 for top-left rotation origin. A concrete workflow: 1) Choose anchor preset that expresses the desired relationship. 2) Adjust Pos X/Pos Y or Left/Right/Top/Bottom offsets to position with margins. 3) Set pivot to control rotation and scale origin. A common mistake is moving an element visually and forgetting to update anchors, which leaves the element with center anchors and leads to unexpected jumps when the parent scales. Test by resizing the Game view and observing whether the element keeps its intended relation. This practice creates robust, responsive layouts without needing manual repositioning for each resolution.

TextMeshPro delivers crisp rendered text and is the recommended component for all UI text. When you add a TextMeshPro element for the first time, Unity prompts you to import the TextMeshPro essentials — do that immediately. After import, create a Text - TextMeshPro element from the UI menu. Set its anchors depending on how you want the text to behave: Top-Center for titles, Center for centered labels, or stretch presets for multi-line bodies. Configure width and height in the Rect Transform; avoid embedding excessive content into a single line. Use the Inspector to set font size, color, and alignment. A concrete example: add a TitleText element, anchor it Top-Center, set Pos Y to -100, and make width about 800 with height 150. This gives consistent placement across resolutions when paired with a Canvas Scaler. A common misconception is that increasing font size alone solves readability on high-resolution displays. In practice, TextMeshPro uses signed distance fields so text remains sharp at different scales; pair it with Canvas Scaler set to Scale With Screen Size to preserve intended visual proportions. After creating text, verify in Game view at multiple resolutions to ensure line wrapping and alignment behave as expected.

Images and Buttons are the visual building blocks of menus and HUDs. To add a background image, right-click Canvas → UI → Image and drag a Sprite into the Source Image field in the Inspector. For backgrounds that must cover the entire screen, set anchors to stretch (Anchor Min 0,0 and Anchor Max 1,1) and set Left/Right/Top/Bottom to zero. Buttons are created via UI → Button - TextMeshPro and combine an Image for the background with a child TextMeshPro label. You can customize the button's Image sprite for different visual styles, and adjust transition settings if you want hover or press feedback. A practical example: create a Play button, set its anchors to Center-Center, set Width 200 and Height 60, and change the child TextMeshPro to say "Play Game." A common mistake is placing the TextMeshPro label outside the button hierarchy or forgetting to assign a sprite to the Image, which results in an invisible button. Always verify that the label is a child of the button and that the button's Image has a valid sprite or color. Finally, test the button in Play mode to ensure visual states and click targets behave as expected.

The UI Hierarchy in Unity determines draw order and grouping. By default, siblings later in the Hierarchy draw on top of earlier siblings. That means to ensure text appears above a background image, place the Text element after or as a child of a container that sits above the Image. Group related elements under an empty GameObject parent such as MainMenuPanel or PlayerHUD to apply shared transforms, anchor sets, and Canvas override behaviors. Parents define coordinate systems for their children through their Rect Transforms; moving or scaling a parent affects all children, which is a powerful way to manage whole panels. A common pitfall is placing a panel under the wrong parent and then wondering why it moves when another object moves. A practical example: create a PlayerHUD parent anchored to the top of the screen, then add health and score as children. Anchoring the parent to top-left keeps all children consistent. Also remember EventSystem appears when you add interactive UI and should remain present for button clicks to work. To check your understanding, rearrange a small set of UI elements and predict which will render on top; then run the scene and verify that draw order matches the Hierarchy.

The Canvas Scaler controls how UI elements scale as the screen size changes. Constant Pixel Size makes elements keep the same pixel dimensions regardless of resolution. For example, with a reference of 1920 x 1080 and Match set to 0.5, Unity balances scaling between width and height so UIs maintain proportions across common aspect ratios.
